mlk-assassination.title: MLK assassination
mlk-assassination.summary: The April 1968 killing of Martin Luther King Jr. John Kiriakou, having set out to read everything he could find on it, concluded that if James Earl Ray fired the shot he was a patsy — citing the implausibility of a lifelong alcoholic making a perfect shot from a flophouse bathroom a block away, and the FBI's documented attempt two years earlier to push King into suicide.
dyk: ...that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) says he set out to read everything he could find about the killing of [Martin Luther King Jr.](/wiki/martin-luther-king) on the principle that if he was going to hold an opinion it *"needs to be an educated opinion"* — and came away believing James Earl Ray was a patsy?

...that [Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) asks why the [MLK assassination](/wiki/mlk-assassination) files were ever classified at all, King having held no office, no clearance and no access to classified information — *"he's a preacher and a civil rights leader"*?
mlk-assassination.body:
The assassination of **Martin Luther King Jr.** in April 1968 is one of three killings covered by the 1992 statute mandating the release of federal assassination records, alongside the [JFK](/wiki/jfk-assassination) and [RFK](/wiki/rfk-assassination) assassinations. [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) treats it as the case where the official account is weakest on its own terms.<Cite t="2:05:39" /><Cite t="2:12:28" />

## From assumption to conclusion

Kiriakou says he began from the conventional view — *"I always believed that James Earl Ray killed Martin Luther King"* — and then decided that *"if I'm going to have an opinion it needs to be an educated opinion,"* reading everything he could get his hands on. His conclusion was that if Ray fired the shot, he was, to borrow Lee Harvey Oswald's word, a patsy.<Cite t="2:12:28" /><Cite t="2:12:59" />

## The case against Ray as lone gunman

The argument Kiriakou makes is one of plausibility rather than forensics. Ray was a man with a well-documented lifelong drinking problem — drunk, in Kiriakou's description, all the time. The vantage point was a run-down flophouse boarding house a full block from the Lorraine Motel, where the rooms had no bathrooms and a single shared bathroom stood at the end of the hall; that bathroom had a long narrow window in the shower with a view of the motel.<Cite t="2:13:29" /><Cite t="2:14:01" />

His summary of what the official account requires: *"we're supposed to believe that this drunk guy with a 40-year-old rifle sat in a public bathroom all day long, nobody ever noticed him, and then he hits the perfect shot from a block away."*<Cite t="2:14:01" />

## The FBI suicide letter

Kiriakou couples the implausibility argument with what he calls a matter of 100 per cent established fact: that two years before the killing the FBI tried to induce King to take his own life, sending him an anonymous letter purporting to come from an African-American man opposed to him, telling him he was a disgrace to Black people and should do the only honourable thing. By all accounts, Kiriakou says, King laughed it off, as he did the accompanying threat to tell his wife he had been unfaithful — common knowledge, in King's own reported reply.<Cite t="2:14:32" /><Cite t="2:15:03" />

Kiriakou stops short of asserting Bureau responsibility, framing it as an open question that the hatred of King inside the FBI in the 1960s makes reasonable to ask: *"perhaps they did it, perhaps they set him up, perhaps they worked with James Earl Ray — we don't know."* Elsewhere he has stated the stronger version, that he believes the FBI rather than Ray alone killed King.<Cite t="2:15:34" />

## Why classified at all

Kiriakou's sharpest question about the withheld files is not what they contain but why they exist as secrets. King held no elected office, no security clearance, and no access to classified information — *"he's a preacher and a civil rights leader, so why would that case be classified in the first place?"* His general principle: *"if this is a criminal act, nothing should be classified."*<Cite t="2:15:34" /><Cite t="2:16:05" />

## A childhood memory of the manhunt

Kiriakou recalls being eight or nine and watching the news coverage of James Earl Ray's escape from prison with his parents, and being shocked by the Americans being interviewed who said they hoped Ray would come to their house so they could hide him — *"he's a hero."* His parents, he says, were appalled.<Cite t="2:16:37" />
